sections.b: The longest shepherd chapter in the Old Testament charges Israel's rulers with eating the flock: they took the fat and the wool, let the weak, sick and lost fend for themselves, and ruled "with force and with crushing cruelty" (Ezekiel 34:4). In response the LORD says, "Here I am", and promises to search for his sheep himself, bring them out of the nations, feed them on the mountains of Israel and judge between sheep and sheep (34:11-22). He then sets over them one shepherd, "my servant David" (34:23). Jeremiah 23:1-8 and Zechariah 10-11 are close companions. John 10 has Jesus take up both roles, shepherd and gate, and 1 Peter 5:2-4 turns the picture on church elders.

common: In the ancient Near East 'shepherd' was a title for a king or ruler, so Ezekiel 34 is an accusation against Judah's kings and leaders.

sections.h: A covenant of peace and a new heart (Ezekiel 34-37)
sections.b: Ezekiel does not speak of a 'new covenant' by name, but his restoration chapters hold its parts. In 34:25 the LORD makes "a covenant of peace" that removes wild animals from the land; in 36:24-28 he gives a new heart and puts his Spirit inside the people so that they keep his rules, and ends with the covenant formula, "You will be my people, and I will be your God"; in 37:26 he makes a "covenant for all time" and puts his sanctuary among them. Read beside Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Deuteronomy 30:6, the passages describe the same change from outside to inside. Ezekiel 18:31 puts it as a command, 'make yourselves a new heart', and chapter 36 as a gift.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 34:25; Ezekiel 36:24-28; Ezekiel 37:26-28; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Jeremiah 32:37-41; Deuteronomy 30:6; Hebrews 8:8-12

sections.b: Ezekiel twice promises a ruler from David's line: one shepherd, "my servant David", who will be "leader among them" (Ezekiel 34:23-24), and a king, "my servant David", who will rule a reunited people, with his descendants "for all time" (37:24-25). The title for the ruler changes: nasi, 'leader', in 34:24 and 37:25, and 'king' in 37:22, 24. Both rest on the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16) and run beside Jeremiah 23:5-6 and 33:14-22. Jewish tradition looks for a Messiah of David's house; Christians read Jesus as the son of David and the good shepherd (Luke 1:32-33; John 10).

Ezekiel 36-39 gives a sequence. God will put "a new spirit" and "my own Spirit" inside his people (Ezekiel 36:26-27). In the valley of dry bones, the same Hebrew word, ruach, is the breath that makes the bones alive (37:5-10), and God says, "I will place my Spirit in you so that you live" (37:14). The sequence ends with the Spirit poured out on the house of Israel, and the end of God's hiding his face (39:29). John 3:5-8 plays on the same double sense of wind and Spirit; Acts 2:17-18 and Titus 3:5-6 apply the images to Pentecost and baptism.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 36:26-27; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Ezekiel 39:29; Joel 2:28-29; John 3:5-8; Acts 2:17-18; Titus 3:5-6

sections.b: Ezekiel is led by the Spirit to a valley of very dry bones and told to prophesy to them. They join, are covered with sinews, flesh and skin, and finally receive breath and stand as a great army. The LORD explains: the bones are the whole house of Israel, who say that their hope is lost, and the graves he will open are the exile (37:11-14). The chapter is a picture of the nation's restoration, and from the first century it was also heard as a promise of the resurrection of the dead. The Talmud records a debate on whether the dead really rose or whether it was a parable (Sanhedrin 92b). Revelation 11:11 echoes 37:5, 10. Jewish communities read the chapter on the Sabbath of Passover, and churches use it at Holy Saturday and Easter.

common: The vision in its own setting is about the restoration of the nation of Israel from the exile.
uncommon: Some Jewish and Christian writers have held that the vision describes an actual resurrection of the dead in Ezekiel's day.

sections.b: Ezekiel's oracle names Gog, 'of the land of Magog', as the chief leader of Meshech and Tubal, who will come from the far north with a coalition from the ends of the earth (Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Beth-togarmah) against a restored Israel living in unwalled villages. It is the LORD who brings him, and the LORD who destroys him with earthquake, mutual slaughter, plague, hail, fire and sulfur (Ezekiel 38:1-23). Israel burns the weapons for seven years and buries the dead for seven months in the Valley of Hamon-gog (39:9-16). Birds and beasts are invited to a sacrificial feast (39:17-20), and the nations learn why Israel went into exile (39:21-29).

sections.h: Names that were read as codes
sections.b: The names have been matched with Goths (Ambrose), Turks (Luther and others), Russians (from the nineteenth century) and others; Augustine refused to name peoples and read Gog and Magog as the nations of the whole earth (City of God 20.11). In Ezekiel the Hebrew phrase can be read 'chief leader of Meshech and Tubal' or 'leader of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal'; the second reading is the basis for the Russia identification. Revelation 20:8 uses 'Gog and Magog' as two nations at the four corners of the earth, gathered after the thousand years. The Qur'an knows Yajuj and Majuj behind a wall (Qur'an 18:94-99).

common: The battle is a vision of God's defense of a restored Israel against a final enemy.
uncommon: Gog is a symbol of all hostile powers and not a nation, as Augustine read it.

sections.b: Ezekiel 35 is a separate oracle against Mount Seir, the hills of Edom. Edom is charged with an 'ancient hatred', with handing Israel's people over to the sword in the hour of their final punishment, and with claiming 'the two nations and the two lands' for itself. The LORD answers, "But the LORD was there." Edom will be a desolation, as Israel was. Chapter 35 pairs with 36:1-15, where Israel's mountains are restored. Obadiah, Psalm 137:7 and Lamentations 4:21-22 charge Edom with the same crime.

The promise to the mountains of Israel ends with the words of the nations: "This land, once desolate, is now like the garden of Eden" (Ezekiel 36:35). Eden stands for the first fruitfulness and safety, now given back. Isaiah 51:3 and Joel 2:3 use the same comparison, and Ezekiel's river from the Temple in 47:1-12 carries the picture further.

"I will sprinkle pure water over you, and you will be clean... I will give you a new heart and place a new spirit inside you... I will put my own Spirit inside you." Ezekiel 36:25-27 is the Old Testament background for the new birth in John 3:5, when Jesus says to Nicodemus, 'a teacher of Israel', that one must be born of water and the Spirit. Titus 3:5-6 and Hebrews 10:22 echo the water and the Spirit. Churches differ on whether the verses describe baptism itself, the work of the Spirit that baptism signifies, or the new birth that precedes it; see the card at Ezekiel 36.

A survivor reaches the exiles with the news that Jerusalem has been struck (Ezekiel 33:21). The chapters after it explain the exile and answer it: the shepherds failed (34), the neighbors who took advantage will pay (35), the profaned name will be hallowed and a new heart given (36), the dead nation will be raised (37), and the last enemy will fall (38-39). The nations will learn that Israel went into exile for its guilt, not because the LORD was weak (39:23), and that his face is no longer hidden (39:29).

sections.h: The holy name profaned and made holy (Ezekiel 36:20-23)
sections.b: Israel profaned the LORD's holy name among the nations: they were called his people but had to leave his land, which made the nations think he was weak. God says he will act, not for Israel's sake but for his holy name, and he will make his great name holy by what he does through them "in front of them" (Ezekiel 36:22-23). The same concern appears in 39:7: "I will never again let it be profaned." Leviticus 22:32 and Isaiah 48:9-11 are the closest parallels.

Ezekiel takes two pieces of wood, writes "Judah's" on one and "Joseph's, the wood of Ephraim" on the other, and holds them together in his hand. The LORD explains that he will gather the Israelites from the nations and make them one nation, one kingdom, under one king, never again two. The sign answers the division after Solomon (1 Kings 12) and gives the old hope for the northern tribes a visible form. Isaiah 11:13 and Jeremiah 3:18 hope for the same. Latter-day Saints read the two pieces of wood as the Bible and the Book of Mormon; see the note at 37:19.

Ezekiel 33:1-9 restates the watchman's duty of 3:16-21: a watchman who sees the sword coming and does not blow the horn bears the blood of those who die, and a watchman who blows it is clear whether or not they listen. The prophet is given this duty again before the news of the fall comes and his silence ends (33:21-22). Acts 20:26-27 and Hebrews 13:17 take the idea to church leaders.

Chapter 33 gives a shorter version of chapter 18 for a people already in exile. The exiles say, "Our rebellions and our sins weigh on us, and we are wasting away in them. How can we go on living?" God swears that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and calls them to turn back; the righteous man who turns to evil loses his standing, and the wicked man who turns and does justice and righteousness lives. To the charge that "the way of the Lord is not fair", God answers that each person is judged by his own ways (33:17-20).

The Hebrew verb shuv, 'turn back', carries the whole chapter: it appears ten times in Ezekiel 33. "As surely as I live, the Lord GOD declares, I take no pleasure in the death of a wicked man. I take pleasure when a wicked man turns back from his way and lives. Turn back, turn back from your evil ways! Why must you die, house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 33:11). The call is open even to a people who believe they are beyond help.

sections.h: The land made unclean, and cleansed (Ezekiel 36 and 39)
sections.b: Ezekiel, a priest, speaks of Israel's conduct as having made the land unclean, "as unclean as a woman during her monthly period" (Ezekiel 36:17), with the blood they shed and their filthy idols (36:18). Restoration is cleansing: God sprinkles pure water on the people (36:25), and after Gog's fall Israel buries the dead for seven months to make the land clean, marking each bone until it is buried (39:12-16). The background is Numbers 19 (corpse uncleanness) and Leviticus 18:24-28 (the land vomits out those who defile it).

Ezekiel's last sign-act in this part is simple and quiet: he writes on two pieces of wood and joins them in his hand. When the people ask what it means, he explains it as the reunion of Judah and the northern tribes under one king (37:18-22). Unlike the sieges and the shaved hair of chapters 4-5, this sign shows a promise, not a threat.

On the fifth day of the tenth month of the twelfth year of the exile, about January 585 BC, a survivor from Jerusalem reaches Ezekiel and says, "The city has been struck!" The fall had come in the summer of 586 (2 Kings 25:3-9). Ezekiel had been told he would hear the news this way and that his mouth would open (24:26-27). Some manuscripts read 'eleventh year'; see the variants.
